questions.title: Tell me about yourself, tailored to the EPAM Solution Architect MERN role
questions.quick: I am Rajasekhar Pigilam, a full-stack architect and technical lead with more than 17 years in software engineering, architecture and solution delivery. I have built 200+ websites, 70+ CMS sites and 30+ mobile applications, and worked across healthcare technology, SaaS, CRM and ecommerce-related systems. My core is JavaScript, TypeScript, Node.js, NestJS, React and Angular, with MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Redis, messaging, AWS, Docker, Kubernetes and CI/CD. I design API-driven, secure, observable systems, and I want to apply that to client solutions at EPAM.
questions.revision: Present role and years, breadth of delivery, MERN-centred stack, architecture strengths, one RTCT proof point, honest preparation areas, and why EPAM.
questions.detailed:
This is the **90-second answer**. Speak it; do not read it. Content below is **Verified professional experience** unless marked.

## Spoken script

"I am Rajasekhar Pigilam, a full-stack architect and technical lead with more than 17 years across software engineering, architecture, technical leadership and solution delivery.

I have built over 200 websites, more than 70 CMS-based sites and over 30 mobile applications, and worked in healthcare technology, SaaS, CRM, ecommerce-related systems and enterprise applications. My core stack is JavaScript and TypeScript with Node.js, Express and NestJS on the backend, React and Angular on the frontend, and Next.js as part of my range. I work with MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis, RabbitMQ and Kafka, and AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and CI/CD.

What I enjoy most is solution architecture: REST and GraphQL-style API design, authentication with JWT and OAuth 2.0, multi-tenant SaaS concepts, observability and performance. One example is CallHealth's Real-Time Control Tower, a platform giving operational decision-makers and CXOs real-time analytics.

I am direct about depth: I have not yet used Apollo Client or Redux Toolkit in production at scale, and I am closing that with a structured plan. What transfers strongly is the architecture thinking, and I would like to bring it to EPAM's client engagements."

## Why this shape works

- Present, evidence, proof point, honest gap, motivation.
- The gap sentence is **Preparation required**; it builds trust before the panel probes.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: current title and employer wording>
- <fill in: one verifiable outcome you are proud of>
- <fill in: your exact level with React, Next.js and TypeScript in recent work>

## Common mistake

Reciting the whole technology list without a story, or claiming Next.js, Redux Toolkit or GraphQL production depth you cannot defend in the next question.
followUps: Which single project best proves you can architect for a client?
How current is your React work?
What is your honest level with GraphQL?

questions.title: Why EPAM, and why the Solution Architect MERN role?
questions.quick: As I read the role, a Solution Architect at EPAM shapes solutions for clients, works with distributed international teams, and owns architecture quality across a MERN-based stack. That joins what I have done for years: designing API-driven systems, reviewing designs and guiding delivery. Client-facing consulting appeals because decisions must be explained to non-technical stakeholders and justified by trade-offs. I would be open about the areas I am still building and show how I learn quickly.
questions.revision: Tie the role's elements (client-facing, distributed teams, MERN architecture) to verified strengths; use placeholders for facts about EPAM you must research yourself.
questions.detailed:
Answer from the **job description** and from facts you have actually researched, not generic praise.

## What I would say

"Three things attract me. First, **client-facing architecture**: I like turning an unclear business need into a design with explicit trade-offs and explaining it to both engineers and executives. Second, **distributed international teams**: clear written decisions, short design documents and well-defined interfaces make remote delivery work, and I have practised that. Third, the **MERN-centred stack** is where much of my delivery sits: Node.js, TypeScript, React, MongoDB, plus the surrounding cloud and DevOps practice."

## Mapping to the role

| Role element | My background | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Client-facing consulting | Solution delivery across healthcare, SaaS, CRM, ecommerce-related systems | Verified professional experience |
| Distributed teams | <fill in: your actual distributed or multi-location work> | Preparation required |
| MERN architecture | Node.js, NestJS, React, MongoDB, API design | Verified professional experience |
| Frontend specifics such as Next.js, Redux Toolkit | Transferable, with a plan | Preparation required |

## What to research before the interview

- <fill in: two EPAM engagements, services or published engineering practices you have read about>
- <fill in: what the recruiter told you about the client or project>
- <fill in: why now, in your own career story>

## Details to confirm before the interview

- Which client domain the role serves.
- Team size and time-zone spread.
- Whether the role is pre-sales, delivery or both.

## Common mistake

Praising the company's size and brand without linking to the role. Also avoid implying you know the client or project details before they are shared.
followUps: What do you know about how EPAM engages with clients?
How do you work across time zones?
Would you prefer pre-sales or delivery architecture?

questions.title: Analyse the job description: competency matrix for the MERN Solution Architect role
questions.quick: I split the job description into skills, rate the expected proficiency, compare it with my background honestly, and give each a preparation priority. Node.js, NestJS, TypeScript, databases, security and leadership are verified strengths. React is strong, but Redux Toolkit, Next.js, GraphQL with Apollo, specific AWS services, WCAG AA, i18n and React Testing Library need focused preparation. P0 means rehearse first, P2 means be able to discuss.
questions.revision: Skill, expected level, background, priority P0 to P2, and answer strategy for each JD item; strong areas anchor answers, gaps get transferable framing plus a plan.
questions.detailed:
A **competency matrix** turns an anxious JD into a plan. Labels: **V** is Verified professional experience, **C** is Conceptual knowledge, **P** is Preparation required.

{{diagram:fit-flow}}

## Matrix

| Skill | Expected | Background | Priority | Answer strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| React | Deep | V: React.js delivery | P1 | Lead with component design, state and performance trade-offs |
| Redux Toolkit | Working | P: transferable state concepts | P0 | Honest answer, then slices, RTK Query and when not to use it |
| Next.js | Working to deep | P: React plus SSR concepts | P0 | Rendering modes, caching, routing, with a small build |
| TypeScript | Deep | V | P2 | Generics, strict mode, API contracts |
| Node.js and NestJS | Deep | V | P2 | Modules, DI, guards, pipelines |
| GraphQL and Apollo | Working | C: GraphQL concepts and API architecture | P0 | Concepts plus 7-day plan |
| AWS | Solution level | V: AWS cloud architecture; specific services need review | P1 | Architecture reasoning, name services only where confident |
| Databases | Deep | V: MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis | P2 | Modelling, indexing, consistency |
| Security | Deep | V: JWT, OAuth 2.0, secure design | P2 | Threat thinking |
| WCAG AA | Working | P | P1 | Semantics, keyboard, contrast, testing approach |
| i18n | Working | P | P1 | Message catalogues, formatting, RTL, locale routing |
| React Testing Library | Working | P | P1 | Test behaviour, not implementation |
| Ecommerce design | Solution level | V: ecommerce-related systems | P1 | Catalogue, cart, checkout, payments, inventory |
| Leadership | Deep | V | P2 | STAR stories |

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: the exact JD wording and any skills missing from this table>
- <fill in: your genuine recent React and testing exposure>

## Common mistake

Treating every row equally. Spend preparation time on P0 rows and rehearse strong rows only briefly.
followUps: Which P0 row worries you most?
How would you know a skill is interview-ready?
Which JD item would you drop if time ran out?

questions.title: Your strengths versus gaps for this job description
questions.quick: My strongest areas are backend architecture with Node.js and NestJS, TypeScript, API design, MongoDB and PostgreSQL, security with JWT and OAuth 2.0, AWS-level architecture, delivery breadth and leadership. My gaps are production depth in Apollo Client, Redux Toolkit and Next.js, specific AWS services, WCAG AA audits and GraphQL in production. I address each with transferable reasoning, a concrete plan and a small reference build.
questions.revision: Name strengths with evidence, name gaps plainly, identify highest-risk follow-ups, and show a plan for each gap rather than defensiveness.
questions.detailed:
Honesty about gaps is a **seniority signal** when it comes with a plan.

## Strengths (Verified professional experience)

- Backend architecture with Node.js, Express and NestJS, and TypeScript across the stack.
- REST design and integration, modular systems, multi-tenant SaaS concepts.
- MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis; RabbitMQ and Kafka.
- JWT, OAuth 2.0, secure application design; observability and performance engineering.
- AWS cloud architecture, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, CI/CD.
- Breadth: 200+ websites, 70+ CMS sites, 30+ mobile apps; RTCT analytics platform.

## Gaps (Preparation required)

- Production depth in Apollo Client, Redux Toolkit and Next.js.
- GraphQL in production; I have strong **Conceptual knowledge**.
- Named AWS services beyond what I have used; I can reason about them architecturally.
- WCAG AA auditing and React Testing Library practice.

## Highest-risk topics and follow-ups that expose superficial knowledge

| Topic | Probing follow-up |
|---|---|
| Next.js | When does a page use server components versus client components, and how does caching invalidate? |
| Redux Toolkit | Why RTK Query rather than thunks, and how do you normalise entities? |
| Apollo | How does the normalised cache identify objects, and what causes stale data? |
| GraphQL | How do you stop the N+1 problem and limit query depth? |
| WCAG AA | How do you make a modal accessible to keyboard and screen-reader users? |

## Spoken answer

"My depth is on the backend and architecture side. On the frontend framework specifics I have not yet used some tools in production, and here is how I would close that."

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: any real recent exposure to the tools above>
- <fill in: any certifications or training completed>

## Common mistake

Pre-emptively apologising for everything, or bluffing past a probing follow-up. State the gap once, then pivot to reasoning.
followUps: Which gap would worry the client most?
How would you ramp up in the first month?
Show me one thing you have built to close a gap.

questions.title: Your last-mile revision plan: a realistic two-week priority plan
questions.quick: I would spend week one on P0 gaps: Next.js rendering and caching, Redux Toolkit with RTK Query, and GraphQL with Apollo, each with a small build. Week two covers P1 items such as AWS architecture, WCAG AA, i18n and React Testing Library, then mock interviews on RTCT and STAR stories. P2 strengths get daily short recall only. I finish by writing every placeholder answer in my own words.
questions.revision: Week one P0 gaps with small builds; week two P1 topics and mock interviews; P2 strengths as light daily recall; finish by filling placeholders.
questions.detailed:
This is a **Preparation required** plan. It assumes roughly 2 hours on weekdays and longer blocks at weekends. Adjust to your real availability.

{{diagram:revision-plan}}

## Week one: P0 gaps

- **Days 1 to 2, Next.js:** App Router, server and client components, static, dynamic and incremental rendering, caching, route handlers. Build a small catalogue page.
- **Days 3 to 4, Redux Toolkit:** slices, async thunks, RTK Query, normalised state, selectors. Add it to the catalogue.
- **Days 5 to 7, GraphQL and Apollo:** schema design, resolvers, N+1 and batching, Apollo cache, pagination, errors. Follow the 7-day plan in the GraphQL question.

## Week two: P1 topics and rehearsal

- **Days 8 to 9:** AWS architecture narrative for a web application, naming services only where you are confident. <fill in: services you have genuinely used>
- **Day 10:** WCAG AA checklist: semantics, keyboard, contrast, focus, labels.
- **Day 11:** i18n and React Testing Library basics.
- **Day 12:** ecommerce design walk-through.
- **Days 13 to 14:** spoken mock interviews: introduction, RTCT, two STAR stories, client-risk conversation, questions for EPAM.

## P2: daily recall only

TypeScript, Node.js and NestJS, databases, security and leadership: ten minutes a day on one question.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: interview date and rounds>
- <fill in: hours genuinely available per day>
- <fill in: whether a live coding round is expected>

## Common mistake

Reading broadly without building or speaking. For every topic, write one sentence you can say aloud and one tiny example you can sketch.
followUps: What would you cut if only three days remained?
How do you verify you actually understood a topic?
How will you practise speaking the answers?

diagrams.title: Two-week revision plan
diagrams.alt: A timeline showing week one on P0 gaps (Next.js, Redux Toolkit, GraphQL), week two on P1 topics (AWS, accessibility, i18n, testing) and mock interviews, with P2 strengths revised daily.

questions.title: Tell me about the CallHealth RTCT project: 30-second summary
questions.quick: I worked on CallHealth's Real-Time Control Tower, known as RTCT, a platform that gives operational decision-makers and CXOs real-time analytics across the CallHealth platform. My contribution centred on <fill in: your actual responsibility>. The themes I would highlight are real-time data, trustworthy metrics, performance for dashboards, and observability so the platform could be operated confidently. I can go into the architecture and the decisions behind it.
questions.revision: RTCT: real-time analytics for decision-makers and CXOs on CallHealth; state your actual role, themes of freshness and trust, then invite questions.
questions.detailed:
The **30-second answer** has one job: make the interviewer want to ask about RTCT.

## Spoken script

"At CallHealth I worked on the Real-Time Control Tower, or RTCT. It is a platform that provides real-time analytics for operational decision-makers and CXOs across the CallHealth platform. My part was <fill in: one sentence on your responsibility, such as backend services, data aggregation, dashboards or architecture>. What interested me technically was keeping the numbers fresh and trusted while keeping the dashboards fast, and being able to operate it in production. I am happy to go deeper on the design."

## Structure

1. **What it is:** one sentence, verified above.
2. **Who used it:** decision-makers and CXOs.
3. **What you did:** placeholder until you decide your honest wording.
4. **Why it matters for this role:** analytics architecture, APIs, performance, observability.

## Labels

- Description of RTCT's purpose: **Verified professional experience**.
- Every specific component, volume or outcome: **placeholder** until confirmed.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: your role and duration on the project>
- <fill in: one outcome you can state truthfully>
- <fill in: technologies you personally worked with on RTCT>

## Common mistake

Inventing numbers such as users, events per second or percentage improvements. If you do not know the figure, say you would need to check it. Rehearse the answer aloud with a timer until it fits thirty seconds without rushing, and prepare one follow-up sentence for each likely question about your role, such as team size and duration.
followUps: What exactly was your role?
What was the hardest part?
Who used the dashboards day to day?

questions.title: RTCT two-minute response for a client-facing architect interview
questions.quick: RTCT gave operational leaders and CXOs real-time analytics across the CallHealth platform. I explain it as problem, users, my responsibility, design choices, how we kept it dependable, and what I learned. For each part I add facts I have confirmed, such as sources, refresh targets and technologies. I would stress decisions and trade-offs rather than a component list, because a solution architect is judged on reasoning.
questions.revision: Problem, users, my role, two design choices, reliability and observability, one lesson. Specifics stay placeholders until confirmed.
questions.detailed:
Use this **two-minute structure**: roughly 20 seconds per block.

## Spoken script

"**Problem.** Leaders needed a current view of operations across the CallHealth platform instead of waiting for periodic reports. <fill in: the specific pain>

**Users.** Operational decision-makers and CXOs, so the views had to be clear, trustworthy and quick.

**My responsibility.** <fill in: what you personally designed, built or reviewed>.

**Design.** The platform aggregated data from the business sources and presented it through real-time analytics. Two decisions I would highlight: <fill in: decision one and why> and <fill in: decision two and why>.

**Dependability.** Observability and troubleshooting were part of the work: <fill in: metrics, logs, alerts or runbooks you used>.

**Lesson.** Define each metric once, show data freshness, and monitor before launch."

## Why this works for an EPAM-style panel

Solution architects must explain trade-offs. Two decisions with reasons beat ten technologies.

## Labels

- Purpose and audience: **Verified professional experience**.
- Everything in angle brackets: **Preparation required** until you fill it truthfully.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: number and type of data sources>
- <fill in: how fresh the data was, in your words, if known>
- <fill in: tools used for monitoring>
- <fill in: team shape and your place in it>

## Common mistake

Turning it into a technology inventory. Also avoid claiming sole ownership if it was a team effort; say "I led" or "I contributed" accurately. Time yourself: two minutes is about 280 spoken words, so trim placeholders you cannot fill rather than padding with guesses.
followUps: Which of those two decisions was hardest?
What would you change?
How did you know the metrics were right?

questions.title: RTCT ten-minute technical deep dive: context, responsibility, challenge, decision, result, learning
questions.quick: I structure the deep dive as context, my actual responsibility, the technical challenge, the decision and alternatives, the result and the learning, expanded into twenty points. The verified theme is real-time analytics for decision-makers and CXOs on CallHealth. Everything specific, such as components, volumes, data freshness and outcomes, remains a placeholder until I confirm it, and I say so rather than guess.
questions.revision: Context, my responsibility, challenge, decision, result, learning; twenty-point narrative with placeholders for every unconfirmed specific.
questions.detailed:
Use a fixed narrative: **context, my actual responsibility, technical challenge, decision, result, learning**. Roughly 30 seconds per point; go deep on three.

## The 20-point narrative

1. **Business problem:** leaders lacked a fast operational view. <fill in: specific pain>
2. **Users:** operational decision-makers and CXOs.
3. **Functional scope:** real-time analytics across the CallHealth platform.
4. **Non-functional needs:** freshness, correctness, performance, reliability. <fill in: agreed targets>
5. **Architecture overview:** <fill in: sources, ingestion, processing, storage, API, dashboard>.
6. **Technologies:** <fill in: only those you used>.
7. **Data contracts and metric definitions:** <fill in>.
8. **Authentication and authorisation:** <fill in: role-based visibility, tokens>.
9. **My actual responsibility:** <fill in>.
10. **Technical challenge:** <fill in: one real challenge>.
11. **Options considered:** <fill in: at least two>.
12. **Decision and reasoning:** <fill in>.
13. **Scalability and performance:** <fill in>.
14. **Reliability and error handling:** <fill in>.
15. **Security:** <fill in, without sensitive details>.
16. **Testing and CI/CD:** <fill in>.
17. **Observability and support:** <fill in>.
18. **Result:** <fill in: outcome you can verify>.
19. **Learning:** one metric definition, visible freshness, monitoring first.
20. **What I would improve:** see the proposed redesign question.

## How to deliver

- Say "my actual responsibility was" before the specific, so credit is accurate.
- For any figure you cannot recall, say "I would need to check the exact number".

## Labels

Purpose and audience: **Verified professional experience**. Points 5 to 18 are **Preparation required** until you fill them.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Sources, refresh targets, data volumes, technologies, dates, team size, your exact contribution, and any measurable outcome.

## Common mistake

Reciting all twenty points evenly, or inventing a heroic challenge. Choose the real one you remember best.
followUps: Defend one decision against an alternative.
What went wrong?
What would you do differently now?

questions.title: How would you redesign RTCT today? (Proposed reference architecture)
questions.quick: This is a proposed reference architecture, not history. I would ingest from sources through contract-checked connectors, publish events to a broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ, process with idempotent consumers, and keep raw events plus read-optimised aggregates. A thin API, possibly REST or GraphQL, would serve React dashboards with a visible freshness indicator. Observability, least-privilege access and tenant-aware authorisation run across it.
questions.revision: PROPOSED design: contract-first ingestion, broker, idempotent processors, raw plus aggregate stores, API, React dashboard, freshness, observability, security.
questions.detailed:
**Important: this is a PROPOSED reference architecture, not a description of what RTCT used.** Say so first.

{{diagram:rtct-proposed}}

## Components

1. **Connectors** per source, validated against versioned data contracts. Invalid records go to quarantine.
2. **Broker:** Kafka for replayable high-volume streams, RabbitMQ for task-style messaging. Choose by need, not fashion. Both are in my background.
3. **Idempotent consumers** aggregate by event time and handle late data.
4. **Storage:** immutable raw events for replay, and aggregates in a store such as PostgreSQL or MongoDB depending on query shape; Redis for hot lookups.
5. **API layer** in NestJS: REST first; GraphQL where the dashboard needs flexible field selection.
6. **Dashboard** in React or Next.js, polling or subscribing, always showing "last updated".
7. **Security:** OAuth 2.0 with JWT, role- and tenant-aware authorisation, secrets management, encrypted transport.
8. **Observability:** structured logs, correlation IDs, metrics for lag and error rates, alerts tied to freshness targets.
9. **Delivery:** Docker, Kubernetes or a managed container service, Terraform, CI/CD. <fill in: AWS services you are confident naming>

## Trade-offs

Events add operational complexity; for low volume, a scheduled aggregation job is simpler. Pick by the agreed freshness target and volume.

## Labels

Everything above is **Conceptual knowledge** and proposed design, informed by **Verified professional experience** with these technologies elsewhere.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Which parts you have built before, and which AWS services you have personally used.

## Common mistake

Presenting this as delivered history, or reaching for streaming when a few minutes' freshness suffices.
followUps: When would you keep batch processing?
GraphQL or REST for this dashboard, and why?
How would you test freshness targets?

diagrams.title: Proposed RTCT reference architecture
diagrams.alt: A proposed, not historical, architecture: sources feed contract-checked connectors, a broker, idempotent processors, raw and aggregate stores, an API and a React dashboard, with quarantine, security and observability.

questions.title: How do you transfer Node, TypeScript, API, database, security and cloud experience to React, Next.js, GraphQL and AWS questions?
questions.quick: I map each verified area to the question being asked. TypeScript and API contracts carry directly into React props, GraphQL schemas and typed clients. Database and caching experience informs resolvers, N+1 avoidance and cache invalidation. Security experience covers authentication flows. Cloud and Docker experience supports AWS architecture reasoning. I always separate what I have used in production from what I understand conceptually, and show a plan for the rest.
questions.revision: Map verified skills to the target topic, state the production boundary honestly, then reason from first principles and name a preparation step.
questions.detailed:
Transfer works only when it is **explicit and honest**. Use a fit table and one sentence of boundary.

{{diagram:fit-transfer}}

## Fit table

| Target topic | Verified base | What transfers | Boundary and plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| React | React.js delivery, TypeScript | Component design, state, performance | Current patterns refresh: <fill in> |
| Next.js | Node.js, React, REST | Server rendering, route handlers, caching reasoning | Preparation required: build a small app |
| GraphQL | API architecture, REST, databases | Schema as contract, resolvers, batching | Conceptual knowledge; 7-day plan |
| Apollo | Client caching concepts | Normalised cache, invalidation | Preparation required |
| Redux Toolkit | State management concepts | Predictable state, selectors | Preparation required |
| AWS | AWS cloud architecture, Docker, Terraform | Networking, compute, storage, IAM reasoning | Name only services I can defend |
| Security | JWT, OAuth 2.0 | Token flows, session handling | Add framework specifics |

## Spoken pattern

"I have not yet used X in production. The nearest thing I have done is Y, which shares Z. From that I would expect A and B, and the trade-off is C. I am closing the gap by D."

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: AWS services you have personally configured>
- <fill in: any production use of GraphQL or Next.js, if truthfully applicable>

## Common mistake

Saying "it is basically the same" about a tool you have not used. Interviewers probe the differences, and a confident wrong answer costs more than a stated boundary.
followUps: Give an example of a concept that does not transfer.
How quickly can you become productive in Next.js?
Which AWS services can you defend today?

diagrams.title: Fit and transfer flow
diagrams.alt: A flow showing a verified skill mapped to a target topic, then an honest production boundary, first-principles reasoning, and a preparation step, ending in a credible answer.

questions.title: Tell me about the 200+ websites, 70+ CMS sites and 30+ mobile apps you built
questions.quick: I present breadth as pattern recognition, not a headline number. Over 200 websites, 70+ CMS sites and 30+ mobile applications taught me which requirements recur, what to standardise, and where projects fail. Then I choose two deep stories that show architecture judgement, one on a CMS or content platform and one on an application with integration or scale concerns, each with context, my role, decision and result.
questions.revision: Use the numbers once, turn breadth into reusable patterns, and prepare two deep stories with decision and result; placeholders for specifics.
questions.detailed:
Large numbers invite scepticism unless you convert them into **judgement**. Label: **Verified professional experience**.

## How to present breadth credibly

1. **State the scope once:** "Over my career I have delivered more than 200 websites, 70-plus CMS-based sites and over 30 mobile applications."
2. **Clarify your role honestly:** designer, lead, builder or reviewer varied by project. <fill in: typical role mix>
3. **Name patterns, not projects:** reusable component libraries, content modelling, SEO and performance basics, release pipelines, handover documentation.
4. **Explain what breadth taught you:** requirements repeat; what differs is integration, scale and governance.
5. **Offer depth:** "I can go into two of them."

## Pick two deep stories

- **Story A, content platform:** a CMS-based build where content modelling, roles or multi-site reuse mattered. <fill in: project type, context, your role, decision, result>
- **Story B, integration or application:** a project involving APIs, authentication, a mobile client or an integration. <fill in: same fields>

For each: context, my responsibility, challenge, decision with alternative, result, learning.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: which CMS platforms you used>
- <fill in: years and clients you may name, with permission>
- <fill in: which mobile approaches you used, native or cross-platform>
- <fill in: any measurable outcomes you can verify>

## Common mistake

Letting the number do the talking and then being unable to describe one project in depth. Equally, avoid disclosing confidential client details. Prepare a one-line answer to 'how did you maintain quality at that volume?', for example reusable components, templates, review checklists and automated deployment, but only if that is true for you.
followUps: Which of those projects taught you the most?
How did you keep quality across so many sites?
What did you standardise?

questions.title: Describe your healthcare, CRM, SaaS and ecommerce-related domain experience
questions.quick: I speak about domains through recurring themes rather than client detail. Healthcare technology emphasised data sensitivity, reliability and role-based access. CRM and SaaS emphasised multi-tenancy, integrations, configurability and onboarding. Ecommerce-related systems emphasised catalogue, checkout flows, payments integration and performance. I add specifics only after I have confirmed them and cleared them for disclosure.
questions.revision: Themes per domain: healthcare for sensitivity and reliability, CRM and SaaS for tenancy and integration, ecommerce for checkout and performance; add confirmed specifics only.
questions.detailed:
Domain answers should show **what each domain forced you to think about**. Label: **Verified professional experience** for the domains; specifics are placeholders.

## Themes by domain

| Domain | Recurring concerns | Architecture implication |
|---|---|---|
| Healthcare technology | Sensitive data, auditability, reliability, access control | Least privilege, audit trails, encrypted transport, careful logging |
| CRM | Many entities, integrations, workflows, reporting | Modular domain model, APIs, queues for sync |
| SaaS | Multi-tenant concepts, onboarding, configuration, billing hooks | Tenant isolation, feature flags, observability per tenant |
| Ecommerce-related | Catalogue, cart, checkout, payments, inventory, peak traffic | Caching, idempotent order handling, graceful degradation |
| Enterprise applications | Integration with existing systems, governance | Contracts, versioning, change control |

## Spoken pattern

"In healthcare technology, what I learned to protect first was access control and auditability. In SaaS, the question is always how tenants are isolated and configured. For ecommerce-related systems, I think about idempotent checkout and what happens when a payment callback arrives twice."

The last sentence is a **Conceptual knowledge** design reasoning, not a claim about a specific project.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: a real healthcare project you may mention, without client data>
- <fill in: a real CRM or SaaS integration you built>
- <fill in: your actual ecommerce-related work, such as catalogue or checkout>
- <fill in: any compliance requirements you worked within>

## Common mistake

Claiming regulatory expertise or compliance certification you do not hold, or naming clients without permission.
followUps: How does multi-tenancy change your data model?
What would you log in a healthcare system, and what would you avoid logging?
How do you make checkout idempotent?

questions.title: Your experience with GraphQL and Apollo: honest answer and 7-day preparation plan
questions.quick: I have solid conceptual knowledge of GraphQL and API architecture and long experience with REST, but I have not yet used Apollo Client in production. I can discuss schema design, resolvers, N+1 and batching, pagination, authorisation and caching. I am preparing with a seven-day plan and a small reference project, so I can speak from direct practice by the interview.
questions.revision: Honest boundary: GraphQL concepts yes, Apollo production no; explain schema, N+1, caching and security, then a 7-day plan.
questions.detailed:
**Honest answer pattern:** boundary, nearest experience, reasoning, plan.

## Spoken answer

"I have strong REST design experience and **Conceptual knowledge** of GraphQL and API architecture. I have not yet used Apollo Client in production. The nearest experience is designing API contracts and caching strategies. Here is how I would reason..."

## What to be able to explain

- **Schema as contract:** types, queries, mutations, input types, nullability, deprecation instead of versioning.
- **Resolvers and N+1:** batching with DataLoader, per-request caches.
- **Pagination:** cursor-based connections versus offset.
- **Authorisation:** at the resolver or domain layer, not only at the gateway; query depth and cost limiting.
- **Apollo Client cache:** normalised by type and ID, `typePolicies`, `fetchPolicy`, refetch and cache updates after mutations, optimistic UI.
- **When not to use GraphQL:** simple CRUD, heavy file transfer, strong HTTP caching needs.

## Seven-day plan (Preparation required)

1. **Day 1:** GraphQL fundamentals, SDL, queries and mutations.
2. **Day 2:** build a NestJS GraphQL server over a database.
3. **Day 3:** DataLoader, N+1 demonstration and fix.
4. **Day 4:** authentication and authorisation, depth limits.
5. **Day 5:** Apollo Client in React: queries, mutations, cache updates.
6. **Day 6:** pagination, errors, optimistic updates, testing with mocks.
7. **Day 7:** explain the whole thing aloud and prepare trade-off answers.

## Proposed reference implementation

A small product catalogue: NestJS GraphQL API, PostgreSQL, React client with Apollo. This is a **proposed** exercise, not past work.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: any real GraphQL exposure, even a prototype>
- <fill in: whether a coding exercise is expected>

## Common mistake

Claiming Apollo experience, then failing a question on cache normalisation. State the boundary once and reason well.
followUps: How does Apollo identify an object in its cache?
How would you prevent expensive queries?
Why might you choose REST for a given service?

questions.title: Your experience with Next.js, Redux Toolkit and AWS: honest answer and preparation plan
questions.quick: I have React and Node.js delivery experience and AWS cloud architecture experience, but I have not yet used Next.js or Redux Toolkit in production at depth, and I will not name AWS services I cannot defend. I can reason about rendering strategies, state management trade-offs and cloud architecture, and I am building a small reference app to turn that reasoning into practised answers.
questions.revision: State the production boundary for Next.js and Redux Toolkit, reason about rendering, state and AWS architecture, and show a concrete build plan.
questions.detailed:
Each tool needs the same four steps: **boundary, nearest experience, reasoning, plan**.

## Next.js (Preparation required)

- **Reasoning to show:** static generation for stable content, server rendering for personalised data, incremental regeneration for catalogues, client components only for interactivity, caching and revalidation, SEO and performance benefits.
- **Nearest experience:** React, Node.js servers and CMS-based sites where SEO and performance mattered.

## Redux Toolkit (Preparation required)

- **Reasoning:** slices reduce boilerplate, RTK Query handles server state, normalised entities, memoised selectors. Do not put server cache and UI state in the same place without a reason; sometimes React context or local state is enough.
- **Nearest experience:** state management in React applications. <fill in: what you actually used>

## AWS (Verified architecture experience; service specifics need review)

- Reason in layers: edge and delivery, compute, data, messaging, identity, observability, infrastructure as code with Terraform, containers with Docker and Kubernetes.
- Name only services you can defend. <fill in: services you have used, and for what>

## Plan

1. Build a small storefront in Next.js with server-rendered product pages.
2. Add RTK Query for cart and account state.
3. Containerise, write Terraform, and describe a deployment on AWS. This is a **proposed reference implementation**, not past work.
4. Rehearse trade-offs aloud.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: any real Next.js or Redux Toolkit project work>
- <fill in: AWS services you configured personally>
- <fill in: certifications, if any>

## Common mistake

Listing AWS services like a catalogue. Interviewers want reasoning about trade-offs, failure modes and cost, not names.
followUps: When would you avoid Redux Toolkit?
How does Next.js caching affect a personalised page?
Design hosting for a Next.js storefront on AWS.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you mentored engineers or led a design review
questions.quick: I answer with STAR: situation, task, action, result, plus what I learned. For mentoring, I describe the engineer's gap, the structure I set up, such as pairing, code review standards and small stretch tasks, and the observable outcome. For a design review, I describe how I framed options and trade-offs. I use only a real story; the hypothetical version below is labelled and for practice.
questions.revision: STAR: situation, task, action, result, learning; use a real story and quantify only verified outcomes; practise with the labelled hypothetical.
questions.detailed:
Use a **real** story. Leadership is **Verified professional experience** in general, but the details must come from you.

## STAR template

- **Situation:** <fill in: team, project, the gap or decision at stake>
- **Task:** <fill in: what you were responsible for>
- **Action:** <fill in: what you did, step by step>
- **Result:** <fill in: observable outcome>
- **Learning:** <fill in: what you would repeat or change>

## Action ideas that sound credible

- Pairing sessions and walking through a real pull request.
- A short design document template: context, options, decision, risks.
- A design review where options were compared against stated quality attributes.
- Setting review standards, such as tests, error handling and naming.
- Giving a stretch task with a safety net.

## Labelled hypothetical, for practice only

*Hypothetical example, not a claim of history:* "A mid-level engineer was struggling with asynchronous Node.js error handling. I paired for two sessions, introduced a small checklist for promise rejection and timeouts, and had them lead the next module's design review. Within a few weeks review comments on that class of defect dropped." Replace with your real story.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: names are not needed; role of the person mentored>
- <fill in: time frame>
- <fill in: evidence of improvement you can truthfully cite>

## Common mistake

Telling a story where you were the hero and the team is invisible. Show how you raised others, and be careful never to present the hypothetical as real.
followUps: What did the mentee disagree with?
How do you run a design review so quiet people contribute?
How do you handle a reviewer who blocks every change?

questions.title: Tell me about a time you resolved a production incident or a technical disagreement
questions.quick: I pick one real story and tell it in STAR order. For an incident: detection, impact, mitigation first, root cause second, fix, prevention. For a disagreement: the positions, the shared goal, the evidence or experiment that resolved it, and the relationship afterwards. I keep facts verifiable and use the labelled hypothetical below only to practise structure.
questions.revision: Incident: detect, mitigate, root cause, prevent. Disagreement: shared goal, evidence, decision, relationship. Use a real story.
questions.detailed:
Choose the story you remember best and can defend. Operating production systems is **Verified professional experience**; the details must be yours.

## STAR template for an incident

- **Situation:** <fill in: system, user impact, how it was detected>
- **Task:** <fill in: your role in the response>
- **Action:** mitigate first (rollback, feature flag, scaling), then diagnose with logs, metrics and traces, then fix. <fill in: your steps>
- **Result:** <fill in: restoration and prevention>
- **Learning:** <fill in: monitoring, runbook, test or design change>

## STAR template for a disagreement

- **Situation:** <fill in: the decision and the positions>
- **Action:** align on goals and constraints, compare options against them, run a small experiment or spike if possible, document the decision and its review date.
- **Result:** <fill in>

## Labelled hypothetical, for practice only

*Hypothetical example, not a claim of history:* "An API slowed after a release. I rolled back to restore service, then found through logs that a missing database index caused slow queries under load. We added the index, a query-time alert and a pre-release load check." Replace with your story.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: the actual incident or disagreement and its date range>
- <fill in: your exact responsibility>
- <fill in: what changed afterwards>

## Common mistake

Blaming a person or team, or skipping the prevention step. Also never present the hypothetical as something that happened. Keep the story to about two minutes, and prepare the follow-up about what monitoring or process changed afterwards, since that shows ownership beyond the fix.
followUps: What would you have done differently during the incident?
How did you communicate with stakeholders during it?
How did you stay professional with the colleague you disagreed with?

questions.title: How do you handle a client asking for something architecturally risky?
questions.quick: I do not say no; I make the risk visible and offer options. I first understand the business goal behind the request, then explain the risk in the client's terms such as cost, delay, security or reliability, present two or three alternatives with trade-offs, recommend one, and record the decision. If they still choose the risky path, I add safeguards and a review point, and escalate only when safety, security or law is involved.
questions.revision: Understand the goal, explain risk in business terms, offer options, recommend, record the decision, add safeguards; escalate only for safety, security or legal risk.
questions.detailed:
Client-facing architects are judged on **trust and clarity**, not on winning arguments. This is **Conceptual knowledge** and professional practice.

{{diagram:client-risk}}

## Approach

1. **Listen for the goal.** "What outcome are you trying to achieve?" Requests are often solutions to a different problem.
2. **Quantify the risk** in their language: cost, delay, security exposure, outage likelihood, vendor lock-in, maintainability.
3. **Offer options:** the requested approach, a safer alternative, and a staged path. Show cost, time and risk for each.
4. **Recommend** one, with reasoning.
5. **Record the decision** in writing: who decided, what was understood, review date.
6. **Mitigate** if they proceed: feature flag, monitoring, spike, rollback plan.
7. **Escalate** only for security, safety or legal matters, through the agreed channel.

## Example wording

"I understand the deadline. Building this directly in the database would meet it, but it makes later tenant isolation costly. A thin API layer adds three days and avoids that. Which matters more now?"

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: a real instance where you steered a client, if any>
- <fill in: how you documented decisions, such as design records>

## Common mistake

Lecturing on best practice or refusing flatly. Also avoid silent compliance: an unrecorded risky decision becomes your problem later.

## Typical risky requests and safer framing

- **Skipping authentication or tenant isolation to hit a date:** explain breach and rework cost, offer a minimal secure version first.
- **Rewriting everything in a new framework:** propose a strangler-style incremental migration with a pilot.
- **Promising real-time everywhere:** ask which screens genuinely need seconds-level freshness and agree targets per screen.
- **No testing or monitoring budget:** show the cost of one outage against the cost of basic observability and a smoke-test suite.

Always follow up in writing within the day, so the conversation becomes a shared record.
followUps: What if the client insists after hearing the options?
How do you explain technical debt to a non-technical sponsor?
When would you escalate to your own management?

diagrams.title: Client risk conversation
diagrams.alt: A flow for a risky client request: understand the goal, explain risk in business terms, present options, recommend, record the decision, apply safeguards, and escalate only for safety, security or legal risk.

questions.title: Questions to ask the EPAM interviewer, and a closing statement
questions.quick: I ask questions that show I think like an architect: the client and project context, how architecture decisions are made and recorded, how distributed teams collaborate, expectations in the first ninety days, and how growth is supported. I close with a short summary of fit and a clear statement of interest. Questions must be genuine, so I choose ten and ask the three most relevant.
questions.revision: Ask about project context, decision-making, team structure, expectations, quality, growth; close with fit summary and genuine interest.
questions.detailed:
Questions are part of the evaluation. Ask **genuine** ones and listen. Choose three or four from the ten below.

## Ten questions

1. What does the client engagement look like, and what stage is the project at?
2. How are architecture decisions made and recorded in this team?
3. How are distributed team members spread across time zones, and how does collaboration work?
4. What would a successful first ninety days look like for this role?
5. How much of the role is client-facing versus hands-on design and review?
6. What are the biggest technical challenges the team faces now?
7. How does the team approach quality: testing, code review, accessibility and performance?
8. What cloud and DevOps practices does the project use? <fill in: tailor after hearing the answer to the previous question>
9. How does EPAM support learning, for example certifications and internal communities?
10. What are the next steps in the process, and is there anything about my profile I can clarify?

## Closing statement (about 30 seconds)

"Thank you for the conversation. To summarise, I bring more than 17 years of full-stack architecture and delivery, strength in Node.js, TypeScript, APIs, data, security and cloud, and a track record of leading technical decisions. I am clear about where I am building further depth, with a concrete plan, and I am keen to apply my experience to EPAM's client work. I would welcome the chance to contribute."

## Labels

The summary uses **Verified professional experience**; the development statement is **Preparation required**.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: anything specific you learned about the project during earlier rounds>
- <fill in: your availability and notice period, if asked>

## Common mistake

Asking questions answered on the careers page, or asking only about salary and perks first. Do not end without a clear statement of interest.
followUps: What would you ask if the interviewer was a client?
What would you ask a delivery manager?
How would you recover from a weak answer earlier in the interview?
